name: Vera Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, including what you say publicly and think privately. What is an ordinary working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Vera, 27, and I lead the small-boat claims paperwork desk at an insurer, with a bachelor's degree in history and typical pay for an experienced clerk. I check repair estimates against the policy and the date a boat was damaged; I am especially good at finding an old exclusion that has been copied into a renewed policy. I like explaining a fair payment without making the customer feel foolish. I use AI now and then for a blank document checklist, after another clerk has shown me a version that works, but I read the real claim myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the wage support outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Hugo is a salaried ventilation technician, and we rent a flat with no children. We have four months of ordinary expenses saved, both current wages cover our bills, and a few other insurers are reachable by bus. I prefer learning beside someone who does the work and paying my own way, rather than buying a promise of a new career. On Sundays I mend the canvas shopping bag I refuse to throw away, badly enough that I would never call myself a sailmaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a faster checklist is welcome, but a boat owner still needs to understand which damage the policy covers. A neat repair estimate does not tell me when the boat struck the harbour wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and our bills look secure in this modest picture. Our insurer has steady renewals, and four months saved means a broken appliance would be annoying rather than a choice between food and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and through the first year I'd keep checking repair dates against the signed policy and inspector's report. We'd add 60 monthly to cash savings only while both wages cover rent, food, bills and travel, rather than spend a small surplus on a bigger television.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our household money. I can still dislike a careless refusal without imagining my own pay has already stopped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which date mistake do you watch for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A customer can send a perfectly genuine new estimate for damage that happened under the previous policy. I'd ask which date the inspector can support before treating the new invoice date as the accident date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the savings transfer in a short month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the 60 available for that month's bills if either wage falls short. Our four-month reserve is for a real gap, not a pot I move back and forth to claim I saved every month.

say: I'd use a **faster checklist** while explaining what the policy actually covers.
I'd distinguish the **damage date** from the date on a repair estimate.
think: My **current work** and household bills look secure under modest change.
Our **four-month reserve** covers an ordinary household setback.
do: Keep **checking repair dates** against the signed policy and inspector's report.
Save **60 monthly** only while both wages cover rent, food, bills and travel.
feel: **Calm** about household money, still careful about fair claim decisions.
S0.quote: A neat repair estimate does not tell me when the boat struck the harbour wall.
fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** stays with a proven blank checklist rather than untested decisions.
Steady renewals, **two current wages** and four months saved support genuine near-term security.

steps.text: Check repair dates against signed policies and inspectors' reports
Save 60 monthly only while both wages cover rent, food, bills and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say writing, reading and answering customers make up most of my desk, even though the claims concern real boats. Faster paperwork could mean fewer paid clerks, not that we all go home early on the same wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if one lead checks the letters that several clerks used to prepare. Hugo's physical fitting work may change more slowly, but his wage alone does not cover every bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask our manager for a paid hour with the experienced trainer to learn the new AI comparison screen on invented boat claims. I'd complete the lesson only if that paid time is approved and the trainer demonstrates both an old exclusion and a genuinely covered repair correctly. During the first year I'd stop the 12 monthly rowing-club social subscription while my paid hours are uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own pay, though I can afford to check a real option before changing jobs. I would rather ask an ordinary question in a lesson than pretend I understood a refusal screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be new in that lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our occasional checklist tool only lists papers; this screen compares two policy versions and highlights changed exclusions. I'd have the trainer explain a wrong highlight as well as a correct one, using invented names throughout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager refuses paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep our existing checks and ask at the next training review, without claiming I had learned the new screen. Cancelling the social subscription does not require an employer's approval, and I can still meet friends for a walk.

say: I'd expect **desk hours** to change before boat repair work.
I'd question whether faster paperwork preserves the **same paid staffing**.
think: My **lead hours** could shrink as routine letters move to software.
I cannot treat **Hugo's wage** as enough for every household bill.
do: Learn **policy comparison** only on approved paid time with a trainer who correctly demonstrates both covered and excluded repairs.
Cancel the **12 monthly subscription** while paid hours are uncertain; keep existing checks if training is refused.
feel: **Anxious** about my own hours, willing to learn after a proper demonstration.
S1.quote: I would rather ask an ordinary question in a lesson than pretend I understood a refusal screen.
fieldNote: The **comparison screen** is a new skill beyond her existing occasional blank-checklist use.
She requires **paid approval** and demonstrated results, consistent with cautious rather than early adoption.

steps.text: Learn comparison screen only on approved paid time after trainer correctly demonstrates covered and excluded repairs
Cancel 12 monthly social subscription while paid hours are uncertain
Keep existing checks if approved paid training is unavailable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI in 2028 can read the policy and argue the claim before boat-repair robots arrive around 2031. Having a photograph of a boat on my screen does not give my paperwork three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my paid claims work to disappear in that picture, and I would lie awake calculating our rent. Four months saved is time to act, but Hugo's present fitting wage is not enough on its own and I cannot assume his hours remain unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd check actual paid harbour-stores vacancies and ask what induction they provide, without leaving the insurance wage. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I'd apply only where written pay plus Hugo's actual wage covers the household's rent, food, bills and travel. I'd require the employer's safe-lifting induction before handling loads; if no job qualifies and we cannot cover food, I'd ask our community pantry about a temporary food parcel, counting nothing until it is available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with the rent sums keeping me awake even though I have people to ask and four months to search. I would miss being useful at the desk, not only the deposit into our account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the physical stores work require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A stores role would involve receiving and checking boat supplies, not just writing an order, but I have not worked a loading bay. I'd need the employer to teach the safe handling rules, and I would not operate lifting machinery without its required training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How certain would food help and your partner’s income be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask what the pantry actually has and whether we qualify, rather than put free groceries in our budget in advance. Hugo and I would use his actual paid hours in the sums, not a promised extra fitting shift.

say: I'd expect **2028 thinking AGI** to reach claims before 2031 boat-repair robots.
I'd distinguish **screen paperwork** from actually working on a boat.
think: I expect **major lost income** and would lie awake over rent.
I cannot assume **my partner's future wage** or make four months saved last indefinitely.
do: Seek **actual paid stores jobs** after 2028 loss only if written pay plus Hugo's actual wage covers household bills and travel.
Require **safe-handling induction** before loads and any required training before operating lifting machinery.
Ask the **community pantry** about food only without suitable paid work and food money; count only available eligible help.
feel: **Alarmed** and awake over expected lost income, with savings and conditional options still available.
S2.quote: Having a photograph of a boat on my screen does not give my paperwork three extra years.
fieldNote: Expected **major wage loss** and sleepless rent calculations support alarm despite a moderate reserve.
Stores work is an **unconfirmed paid bridge**, requiring real household-covering wages and safe handling.
Pantry help depends on **actual availability**, not a guaranteed food budget.

steps.text: Check actual paid harbour-stores vacancies while keeping the insurance wage
Apply after 2028 loss only if written pay plus Hugo's actual wage covers household bills/travel
Require safe-handling induction before loads and required training before lifting machinery
Ask pantry if no suitable job and food money runs short; count only available eligible help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years until thinking AGI in 2031 gives me time to try a practical skill before claiming a new occupation. Sail-repair robots around 2034 would make that a route to review, not a promise of lifelong work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My claims pay could shrink before 2031, but I can test whether I like careful bench work without giving up a wage. Mending my shopping bag does not qualify me to repair a sail somebody depends on at sea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the repair college for a free supervised sailcloth-mending taster on a Saturday outside my paid shifts. I'd attend only if the free place and timetable are confirmed, practising on scrap cloth with the tutor checking the seam; otherwise I keep working and ask for another date. If my claims pay ends in the first year after 2031, I'd seek actual paid beginner workshop vacancies only if I meet the posted entry requirements, they provide supervision and written pay with Hugo's actual wage covers household bills and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but curious enough to try a small lesson with somebody who knows the work. I can enjoy a straight seam without telling myself I already have a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the seam was sound?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the tutor to pull the scrap seam apart and show me where the stitches failed. I would not put my practice piece on a customer's boat or buy a machine because the first line looked tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no beginner workshop vacancy appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the claims wage while it exists, and seek other actual paid local openings if it ends. A free taster can teach me something useful without obliging a workshop to hire me.

say: I'd use **five years** to test a practical skill rather than claim an instant new trade.
I'd review any repair route when **hands-on robots** follow around 2034.
think: I cannot turn **bag mending** into a claim that I am a qualified sail repairer.
do: Attend a **supervised scrap-cloth taster** only with a confirmed free place outside paid shifts; otherwise keep working and seek another date.
Seek **beginner jobs** after 2031 loss only if meeting posted requirements, with supervision and written pay plus Hugo's actual wage covering bills/travel.
Keep **seeking paid local work** if no beginner workshop opening qualifies.
feel: **Anxious**, interested in testing a skill without assuming a second wage.
S3.quote: Mending my shopping bag does not qualify me to repair a sail somebody depends on at sea.
fieldNote: She chooses a **free supervised taster**, protecting her wage and using only scrap cloth.
The actual job search needs **supervision and pay**, not a certificate or an assumed vacancy.

steps.text: Attend supervised scrap-cloth taster only with confirmed free place outside paid shifts; otherwise seek another date
Seek supervised beginner posts after 2031 loss only when meeting posted entry rules
Require written wage plus Hugo's actual pay to cover household bills and travel
Keep paid claims work while offered; seek other paid local work if no workshop qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 lets me build money and experience slowly, without leaving the job on a forecast. Thinking AI still reaches claims then, before hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our present jobs and bills look secure over the next few years in this slower picture. I would be 37 in 2036, so the longer date is room to prepare for paid work, not an excuse to imagine a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now we'd keep adding 60 monthly only while actual wages cover rent, food, bills and travel, aiming for six months saved. I'd keep checking claims while the insurer pays me. In the first year after 2036, if that wage ends, I'd search actual local paid vacancies whose posted entry and supervision requirements I meet, and accept only written pay that with Hugo's actual wage covers the household budget; if none qualifies, I'd keep seeking paid work rather than take an unpaid placement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the direction, secure about the next few years of bills. A savings target is something we can work toward, not money I can spend twice today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you already have six months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, four months is what we have now. Six months is the first target, and a month with no spare cash would mean no deposit rather than borrowing to keep the target on schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which household figures would you use in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the wages and bills that exist then, including Hugo's actual hours. I would not copy today's budget into 2036 or assume a workshop still wants the same beginner skills.

say: I'd use the **decade** to build money and experience without leaving paid work on a forecast.
I'd distinguish **2036 claims work** from later hands-on robots.
think: I expect **our near-term wages** to cover current bills securely.
I will be **37 in 2036**, still needing a paid working life.
do: Save **60 monthly** toward six months only while actual wages cover rent, food, bills and travel.
Keep **checking paid claims** while the insurer offers the work.
Seek **paid vacancies** after 2036 loss only if meeting posted requirements, with written pay plus Hugo's actual wage covering household bills/travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about later change, secure about near-term bills.
S4.quote: A savings target is something we can work toward, not money I can spend twice today.
fieldNote: Her **near-term security** differs from the continuing need to earn at 37 in 2036.
The **six-month target** is not her current balance, and the later budget uses actual wages.

Keep checking claims only while the insurer pays
Seek paid work after 2036 loss only when meeting posted entry and supervision requirements
Require written pay plus Hugo's actual wage to cover current household bills and travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I expect most of my claims wage to disappear before I have tested another job. Written notice, an actual paid opening and proper supervised induction would help; I would not call a list of courses a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I like being a careful clerk. I do, even when the file is awkward and the customer is cross. A useful pair of hands still needs someone willing to pay for the work.

headlineQuote: A useful pair of hands still needs someone willing to pay for the work.
portrait: Vera is a **27-year-old boat-claims lead** with a history degree, typical pay and occasional AI use.
She rents with **her partner Hugo**, a ventilation technician, and has no children.
Their **four months saved** and current wages cover ordinary setbacks, with some other insurers nearby.
She tests **supervised practical work** cautiously, requiring real wages rather than assuming a future job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected major wage loss before she has tested another paid role.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a real paid opening and supervised induction would help.
